slides.say: A semicircle has center K and radius r. M and N lie on its curved boundary, and angle K M N is sixty degrees. What is the ratio of the perimeter of the semicircle to the perimeter of triangle K M N?

So they ask for the perimeter of the semicircle, divided by the perimeter of the triangle. [short pause] There's a triangle inside a semicircle here. In questions like this, we write the lengths of both shapes with the radius of the circle.
at: So they ask for the perimeter

slides: We'll solve it the math way, then by plugging in numbers, and then by estimation. At the end, we'll look at two of the choices by understanding.

slides.say: [short pause] The math way first. K M and K N are radii, so each one is r. So the triangle is at least isosceles, and its base angles are equal.
at: K M and K N are radii

slides.say: The angle at M is sixty, so the angle at N is sixty too. That leaves sixty for the angle at K. An isosceles triangle with a sixty-degree angle is equilateral, so M N is r too.
at: the angle at N is sixty
so M N is r too

slides.say: So the perimeter of the triangle is r plus r plus r, three r.
Now the semicircle. A lot of students take half of the circumference. That's only part of it. The perimeter has two parts, the curved part on top and the straight line at the bottom.
The curved part is half of the circumference. The circumference is two pi r, and half of it is pi r.
at: and half of it is pi r

slides.say: The straight line is the diameter, two radii, so it's two r. So the perimeter of the semicircle is pi r plus two r.
at: The straight line is the diameter
So the perimeter of the semicircle

slides.say: Now we divide. Pi r plus two r, over three r. In the top, take r out as a common factor. That gives r times the whole bracket, pi plus two, all over three r. Now r is multiplied on the top and on the bottom, so we cancel it. We get pi plus two, over three. Choice number three is our answer.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's plug in numbers. Instead of the letter r, we pick an easy number for the radius, and we solve with numbers. Then we put the same number into the choices. The right choice gives the same value. It also saves us algebra mistakes.
The easiest number is one, so the radius is one. K M and K N are one, and the triangle is equilateral, so M N is one too. The triangle's perimeter is three.
The semicircle has a curved part, half of two pi, which is pi. And the diameter is two. So the ratio is pi plus two, over three.
at: So the ratio is pi plus

slides.say: Now we put r equals one into the choices. Choice number one is pi over three. That's not our value, so it's out. But in choices two, three and four, multiplying or dividing by one changes nothing. All three give pi plus two, over three.
at: Choice number one is pi over three

slides.say: So r equals one ruled out one choice, but three remain. To break the tie, let's try another easy number, r equals two.
[short pause] Here's the figure again, with radius two. The triangle is two, two and two, so its perimeter is six. The curved part is half of two pi times two, so it's two pi. The diameter is four.
So the ratio is two pi plus four, over six. Divide the top and the bottom by two, and it's pi plus two, over three.
at: So the ratio is two pi
Divide the top and the bottom by two

slides.say: Now r equals two in the choices. Choice number two says pi plus two, over three r. Three r is six, so it's pi plus two, over six. That's half of our value, so it's out. Choice number four says r times the whole bracket, pi plus two, all over three. With r equals two, it's twice our value. It's out too.
at: With r equals two, it's twice

slides.say: Only choice number three gives pi plus two, over three. Choice number three again.
[pause] And the third way, estimation. Say the radius is one again. The triangle is equilateral, so each of its sides is one, and its perimeter is three.
at: Say the radius is one again

slides.say: Now the curved part. Let's draw two new helper radii, K U and K V. They cut the semicircle into three equal sectors. Three times sixty is a hundred eighty, so each sector has sixty degrees at K. These are new lines, not K M and K N.
at: Let's draw two new helper radii

slides.say: Each small triangle has two radii and a sixty-degree angle between them, so it's equilateral. So the straight line under each arc is one.
at: So the straight line under each arc

slides.say: And a straight line is the shortest way between two points. So each arc is longer than its chord. Each arc is more than one.
at: Each arc is more than one

slides.say: So the curved part is more than three. Add the diameter, two, and the semicircle's perimeter is more than five. The triangle is three. So the ratio is more than five thirds.

the semicircle's perimeter is more than five

But look. Here's the same figure, and next to it the same figure twice as big. Every length is twice as long, so both perimeters are twice as big.

The semicircle goes from pi plus two to two pi plus four, and the triangle goes from three to six. When we divide, the two cancels. So when we make the figure bigger or smaller, the ratio doesn't change.
